For those confused by the theme or who think it is inconsistent, let me clarify:
The theme is SIZE UP. Four words are changing by changing a size in the word one size up.

EXSPOUSES—ESPOUSES (XS-S)
AQUARIUS—AQUARIUM (S-M)
MOBSTERS—LOBSTERS (M-L)
ALES—AXLES (L-XL)

Nobody said or implied that the resulting fill must have the same number of letters and it doesn’t in two answers, one smaller and one larger. Arguably you could have done a rebus for AXLES but that would have been inconsistent and unnecessary.

Tricky? Yes? Unconventional? yes. Inconsistent? I don’t see how.

I don’t know the exact parameters, but the period of comparison with previous puzzles for the sake of the overall rating comes from the puzzles immediately preceding it (a matter of weeks or months), and I think it gets frozen shortly after the puzzle is published. It’s in the fine print, but that’s what can make an old “Hard” puzzle with a median solve of 52 minutes, and “Hard” now with only a median of 25 minutes. Noise or no noise, some of those old puzzles have a median of over an hour, and that’s never the case now. 

In any case, xwstats is the only actual data we can look at, and I’m grateful that someone is compiling them. 

Across Lite was a third-party app that is no longer being linked to the NYT site. It wa very basic; it could not handle the occasional trick puzzle. The software they use now is proprietary. I don’t know how gathering data from one or the other affects the solve times. 

But like when you compare the baseball statistics of Ruth and Ohtani, you do it despite knowing there’s got to be some noise. The Babe rode trains to away games, after all, and his training diet was hot dogs!

Sometimes people will post data from xwstats.com. One thing I noticed that throws off the data: If you refresh it on the profile page to add puzzles beyond the last 60 days, any puzzle that you have started but not finished will be recorded as a time of 0:00.

Even if you go back and finish a puzzle and refresh again, that time is still locked in at 0:00. It does NOT update to your actual solve time.

This leads me to believe that the solve data for the historical puzzles is probably off.

A note on AI and LLMs:

I tend to think of LLM as an alternate name for AIs, not a variety of it.  And I prefer to use LLM, because it's not clear to me that computers are intelligent.  They're very good at solving problems, but IMHO intelligence implies consciousness, and it's clear to me that computers don't possess consciousness.  They merely possess complicated algorithms for predicting the next word to be uttered.

An old calculator can solve many math problems, but would you say it has intelligence?  How about a slide rule?

(If computers were to become "conscious", there are a number of fascinating ethical questions that would arise.  Would a computer have rights?  Would it have responsibilities?  Could we treat them like slaves?  Would it be murder to throw one out or even turn it off?)

I know it's a losing battle, but I advocate using LLM and ditching the acronym AI.
[And if Al in Pittsburgh is reading this, I hope I haven't offended.]

Why have crossword puzzles become less and less about words and more about ostensibly clever gimmicks?  Decades of solvers were happily challenged by constructors who managed to find ways to create puzzles that were crossword puzzles.  These days, puzzles are more often about gimmicks and less about the words, especially later in the week.  Yes, there are still "old-fashioned"  puzzles that are intrinsically challenging, but far more often constructors seem to rely on gimmicks that contribute little to the pleasure of solving the puzzle.
